planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in humus-rich, well-drained soil in full sun; this deciduous species dies back completely in winter, which is part of what allows it to survive colder conditions than evergreen agapanthus.

directions: A southern African species distinguished by a notably long, thickened flowering stem that continues to elongate below the umbel even after the blue flowers have opened, giving mature clumps a taller, more architectural presence than many garden hybrids. Grow in humus-rich, well-drained soil in full sun to light afternoon shade, and let the strap-shaped leaves die back naturally each autumn without cutting them prematurely, since they continue feeding the fleshy roots. Established clumps resent frequent disturbance and flower more heavily when left undivided for several years. Winter mulch over the crown extends its reliability toward the colder edge of its hardiness range.

common_name: Baby Pete Agapanthus (Dwarf Reblooming Lily of the Nile)

planting.note: Plant container-grown starts in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; Baby Pete stays compact and dense, making it well suited to small beds, mass edging, and containers.

directions: One of the smallest evergreen agapanthus in general cultivation, forming a dense, tidy mound of narrow strap foliage barely a foot tall, with short scapes carrying rounded blue umbels that appear over a longer stretch of the growing season than most agapanthus rather than in one concentrated summer flush. Its diminutive scale suits raised beds, mixed containers, and tight border edges where larger agapanthus selections would overwhelm the space. Grow in full sun in well-drained soil, water deeply but infrequently once established, and expect the heaviest bloom from clumps that are left to fill in and become slightly congested. Remove spent scapes at the base to encourage continued flowering.

common_name: Loch Hope Agapanthus (Tall Late-Blooming Violet-Blue Lily of the Nile)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Loch Hope dies back to the crown each winter and emerges late, so mark its location to avoid disturbing dormant roots.

directions: A Scottish-raised deciduous selection bred for combining substantial height and an unusually late, long-lasting flowering season with reliable cold hardiness well beyond that of the evergreen species. Dense, rounded heads of deep violet-blue trumpet flowers top sturdy scapes well above the clump in late summer, extending the agapanthus display after earlier cultivars have finished. Grow in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil, and mulch the dormant crown in winter at the colder end of its range. Because it flowers most heavily once established and slightly crowded, avoid dividing clumps more often than every four to five years.

common_name: Getty White Agapanthus (Robust White Lily of the Nile)

planting.note: Plant container-grown divisions in spring in well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; Getty White forms vigorous, wide-spreading clumps well suited to large-scale mass plantings.

directions: A vigorous, heavy-blooming white-flowered selection popularized in large Southern California public plantings for its dense clumps of broad, dark evergreen foliage and abundant, tall scapes topped with clean white umbels each summer. Its robust growth rate and heavy flower production make it a strong choice for mass landscape beds, median plantings, and large mixed borders where a bold white accent is wanted against darker foliage. Grow in full sun to light afternoon shade in well-drained soil, and allow clumps to become well established and moderately crowded before considering division, since flowering is heaviest on mature stands. Drought-tolerant once rooted in, it needs only occasional deep watering through the summer bloom period.

common_name: Neverland Agapanthus (Variegated Foliage Lily of the Nile)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Neverland holds its cream-and-green striped variegation best with some protection from the most intense midday sun.

directions: A compact evergreen selection grown primarily for its bold, cream-striped foliage, which provides season-long ornamental interest well before the clear blue summer umbels appear on upright scapes above the clump. The variegation is most vivid on plants given a little relief from the harshest afternoon sun, though full sun is tolerated in milder coastal climates. Grow in well-drained soil, groom out any all-green reverted leaves promptly at the base to keep the clump true to type, and avoid dividing until the clump is well filled in, since flowering and foliage color are both best on established plants. Its smaller stature suits containers and foliage-focused mixed borders.
